8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":20,"verseId":5,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Cause and Effect (Saṃbhava)","totalVerses":24,"verseData":{"id":"v20_5","number":5,"title":"The Cause's Double Nature: Causal Status Lost After Production","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If the cause, in having its effect, Ceased to have its causal status, There would be two kinds of cause: With and without causal status."},"philosophy":{"insight":"Beginning the temporal analysis (vv.5-11): if a cause INHERENTLY loses its \"causal status\" after producing its effect, it has TWO contradictory inherent natures: (1) being-a-cause (before production) and (2) not-being-a-cause (after production). But inherent nature (svabhāva) is by definition unchangeable. An inherent cause can't become an inherent non-cause.","madhyamaka":"Hetu phale kṛte hetutvam vihāya (cause, having produced the effect, gives up its causal nature): if this is inherent, the cause has two svabhāvas (being-a-cause, not-being-a-cause). But svabhāva is unchangeable — what inherently IS a cause can't inherently STOP being a cause. The \"two natures\" contradict the very concept of inherent essence.","quantum":"Quantum measurement: the measuring apparatus changes state after measurement — but this change is understood as a dynamic process, not a change in inherent nature. The apparatus doesn't have two \"inherent\" natures. Like v.5: inherent change in causal status is problematic; conventional change is fine.","bridge":"Both quantum measurement and v.5 address the problem of state change. QM: measurement changes the system (conventionally, not inherently). V.5: the cause changing its causal status (inherently) creates two contradictory natures. Both: change is real conventionally but can't involve changing inherent essence.","accessible":"A teacher who becomes a \"non-teacher\" the moment they finish a lesson — do they have two natures? If being a teacher was their INHERENT nature, they can't lose it. If they can lose it, it wasn't inherent. The problem: inherent properties can't be gained or lost.","twoTruths":"Conventionally: causes DO \"lose\" their causal role after production — seeds become sprouts, and the seed is no longer functioning as a cause. Ultimately: this conventional change doesn't involve inherent natures being gained or lost. Conventional roles change; inherent essences (if they existed) couldn't.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying causes don't conventionally cease after producing effects. Seeds conventionally become sprouts. The verse challenges the INHERENT version: an inherent cause can't inherently change to a non-cause. Conventional change is fine; inherent change is contradictory."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"State Change Without Inherent Nature Change","score":50,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Quantum measurement changes a system's state (conventionally) but doesn't change its \"inherent nature.\" V.5: an inherent cause can't lose its inherent causal status without contradiction. Both: change occurs conventionally, not in inherent essences.","caveat":"Quantum state change is a physics process. V.5 is about inherent nature. The parallel is about the impossibility of inherent nature change."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A cause labeled \"CAUSE\" producing an effect. The \"CAUSE\" label then tries to change to \"NOT-CAUSE\" — but the transition flickers, highlighting the contradiction. Two natures can't both be inherent.","educationalGoal":"User sees: inherent causes can't become inherent non-causes. If they could change, they weren't inherent in the first place."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why can't an inherent cause lose its causal status?","a":"Inherent nature (svabhāva) is by definition unchangeable — it's what something IS from its own side, independently, permanently. If the \"cause\" could become \"non-cause,\" its nature changed — but inherent natures CAN'T change. The concept of inherent essence contradicts the concept of change.","realLifeExample":"If being human is your inherent nature, you can't become non-human. If you could, \"being human\" wasn't your inherent nature. Same for causes: if a cause can become a non-cause, \"being a cause\" isn't inherent."},{"q":"What is the \"double nature\" problem?","a":"The cause would need TWO inherent natures: (1) cause-nature (producing effects) and (2) non-cause-nature (after production). But a thing can't have two contradictory inherent natures. This is like saying a square is inherently a circle — contradiction.","realLifeExample":"A coin can't be inherently \"heads\" AND inherently \"tails.\" It can show either side conventionally, but both can't be its permanent, inherent nature."},{"q":"How does this begin the temporal section?","a":"VV.1-4 examined spatial relation (effect in/not in cause). VV.5-11 examine temporal relation: what happens to the cause AFTER production (v.5), BEFORE production (v.6), DURING production (v.7), and what happens if the effect arises BEFORE the cause (v.8). Each temporal option fails.","realLifeExample":"After examining WHERE the suspect was (spatial, vv.1-4), the investigation examines WHEN (temporal, vv.5-11). Both analyses find problems with the inherent-existence hypothesis."},{"q":"What is the conventional solution?","a":"Conventionally, causes DO change status: the seed \"becomes\" the sprout, the match \"becomes\" the flame. These are conventional changes in conventionally designated entities — no inherent natures are gained or lost because there are no inherent natures to begin with.","realLifeExample":"An actor plays a king, then plays a beggar. They \"change nature\" conventionally (role) without changing inherent nature (they're always an actor). Causes similarly change role without changing inherent nature — because they have no inherent nature."},{"q":"How does this relate to Ch.7 (arising/ceasing)?","a":"Ch.7 showed that arising and ceasing can't be inherent. V.5 applies this to causation: the cause \"ceasing to be a cause\" is problematic if inherent. Ch.7 + Ch.20 v.5: inherent change (of any kind) is impossible. Only conventional change works.","realLifeExample":"Same tool (no inherent change) applied to different objects: Ch.7 applies it to phenomena; Ch.20 v.5 applies it to causes. Same result: inherent change is impossible."},{"q":"What comes next?","a":"V.6: what if the cause ceases BEFORE producing the effect? V.7: what if cause and effect are simultaneous? V.8: what if the effect arises before the cause? Each temporal option will be shown to fail for inherent causation.","deeper":"V.5 initiates the temporal section of Ch.20 (vv.5-11) by examining what happens to the cause's inherent status after production. The problem is fundamental: inherent existence (svabhāva) is by definition unchangeable. Any \"change\" in inherent nature is a contradiction. This means: either the cause is ALWAYS a cause (permanent — never ceasing to produce) or it was NEVER a cause (never had causal nature). There's no coherent way for an inherent cause to become an inherent non-cause. This temporal argument complements the spatial arguments of vv.1-4: inherent causation fails across space AND time."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Why can't an inherent cause lose its causal status?","options":["A) It can","B) Inherent nature is unchangeable by definition. If the cause could become a non-cause, its nature changed — contradicting inherence. Two contradictory natures can't both be inherent.","C) Causes are permanent","D) Causes have no status"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Inherent = unchangeable. If it changes, it wasn't inherent. Two contradictory inherent natures = logical contradiction."},"intermediate":{"question":"How does v.5 begin the temporal analysis of causation?","options":["A) It doesn't","B) V.5 examines what happens to the cause AFTER production. VV.6-8 will examine before, simultaneous, and prior. Together: every temporal relation between inherent cause and effect fails.","C) Only spatial matters","D) Time is irrelevant"],"correct":"B","explanation":"After (v.5), before (v.6), simultaneous (v.7), effect-first (v.8). Every temporal option for inherent causation fails."},"advanced":{"question":"How does the \"double nature\" problem connect to svabhāva?","options":["A) No connection","B) Svabhāva (inherent nature) is by definition unchangeable, independent, and permanent. A cause having TWO svabhāvas (cause, then non-cause) contradicts the very concept — svabhāva can't change. This shows inherent causation is logically incoherent.","C) Svabhāva allows change","D) Double nature is fine"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Svabhāva = unchangeable. Two contradictory svabhāvas = impossible. Inherent cause → inherent non-cause violates the definition of inherent nature."}},"verseText":"If the cause, in having its effect, Ceased to have its causal status, There would be two kinds of cause: With and without causal status.","madhyamakaConcept":"Hetu phale kṛte hetutvam vihāya (cause, having produced the effect, gives up its causal nature): if this is inherent, the cause has two svabhāvas (being-a-cause, not-being-a-cause). But svabhāva is unchangeable — what inherently IS a cause can't inherently STOP being a cause. The \"two natures\" contradict the very concept of inherent essence.","quantumPhysicsParallel":"Quantum measurement: the measuring apparatus changes state after measurement — but this change is understood as a dynamic process, not a change in inherent nature.
